subject: business-studies
title: SWOT Analysis Adventure
meta_desc: Business Plans Adventure 3 — KS3 Business Studies on SWOT analysis for new businesses.
final_note: You learned SWOT and how to use it to size up a business idea.

concepts.def: Something you do well inside the business
A chance from outside the business

walkthroughs.body_html:
Strengths and weaknesses are internal.

  • Strength — a famous brand, great staff.
  • Weakness — high costs, slow website.

You can change these yourself. ✨

Opportunities and threats come from the outside world.

  • Opportunity — new trend (vegan boom).
  • Threat — new competitor opens nearby.

You can't change them; you respond.

Make a 2x2 grid. Be honest!

Plan to:

  • Use strengths.
  • Fix weaknesses.
  • Grab opportunities.
  • Dodge threats.

SWOT is the founder's compass. 🧭

mcqs.q: A new rival opening nearby is a…
How do stakeholder and shareholder interests overlap and conflict?
options: Shareholders are a subset of stakeholders. Their interests overlap (long-term success benefits all) but conflict on issues like dividends vs investment, wages vs profits, or short-term gains vs long-term sustainability.
Stakeholders and shareholders always want the same thing.
ROCE is the wages divided by hours worked.
Shareholders are external and stakeholders are internal.

mcqs.q: How is Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) calculated?
options: Operating profit divided by capital employed (total equity + non-current liabilities), expressed as a percentage. It measures how efficiently the business uses its long-term financing to generate profit.
Shareholders are external and stakeholders are internal.
ROCE is the wages divided by hours worked.
ROCE is just net profit divided by revenue.

mcqs.q: What do McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y describe?
options: Theory X and Theory Y are stages of business growth.
Theory X is about working in a factory and Theory Y is about office work.
Shareholders are external and stakeholders are internal.
Two contrasting management assumptions: Theory X assumes workers dislike work and need control; Theory Y assumes workers can be self-motivated and seek responsibility.
